title: The tablet
hook: the first thing anyone writes is a letter: Guru Nanak's Patti, a poem with one line of wisdom for each Gurmukhi letter

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Oankar, an alphabet that asks a teacher to listen. Your line was humble learning.

What was the first thing you ever wrote? Not a sentence. A letter. One shape, traced over and over, probably crooked. Before anyone writes a word, they learn the marks one at a time. Yesterday's poem sang the alphabet to a scholar. Today's takes it back to the beginner's desk. In Raga Asa, Guru Nanak has a poem named for the thing a child wrote on. Its name is Patti.
screen: `THE FIRST THING YOU EVER WROTE.` → `ONE SHAPE AT A TIME.` → `BACK TO THE BEGINNER'S DESK.`

segments.voice: Patti means a tablet, a writing board. Earlier on this path we heard the janamsakhi story of the boy Nanak at school, asking his teacher what the letters really point to. Today we open the poem itself. First, its shape. The Patti is an acrostic: each stanza opens with a letter of the Gurmukhi alphabet, and that letter starts a line about God and the soul. Letter by letter, the alphabet becomes a path. Second, how it begins. It opens with sasai, the letter S, and a line about the One who made the world, which we take up tomorrow. Then eevrri, in paraphrase: the Primal Being is the Giver, and that One alone is true. Then oorrai: praise the One whose limit no one has found. Three letters in, the poem has said who made things, who gives, and that the giver can't be measured. Third, why a tablet. A writing board is where learning starts small. You don't begin with a library. You begin with one mark, then the next. The Patti keeps that pace on purpose: one letter, and one line of wisdom to go with it. That's a way to learn anything deep: not all of it today, just the next letter. Fourth, the plain humility of the form. A writing board belongs to beginners, and the poem carries its name. The tablet stays a tablet. It just points further.
screen: `PATTI: A WRITING BOARD.` · `AN ACROSTIC: ONE LETTER, ONE LINE.` · `IT OPENS WITH SASAI.` · `LEARNING AT THE PACE OF ONE MARK.` · then, large: `LETTER BY LETTER.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and any scrap of paper and copy the three letters the Patti opens with, sasai, eevrri and oorrai, slowly, the way a beginner would, saying each name softly; if Gurmukhi isn't open to you right now, write the first three letters of any alphabet you know, just as slowly. Don't judge how they look. Then put the pen down and sit with your breath, and if you pray, say Waheguru once.
Patti. A writing board, and Guru Nanak's poem in Raga Asa that gives each Gurmukhi letter a line of wisdom. Today's word.
Your line: letter by letter. Nothing deep is learned all at once. One mark, then the next.

howItsDone: In gurdwara Punjabi classes and at home, children learn the Gurmukhi letters, and teachers sometimes use the Patti to show that each letter can carry a line of the Guru's teaching.

chat.says: Why would a Guru write a poem about the alphabet?
options: Each letter starts a line about God, so you learn it one letter at a time.
To teach kids spelling; the Patti is a school primer, not a hymn.
Because only people who read Gurmukhi are allowed to pray.
